core.text: Deponents build their participle like everyone else, but it means the opposite: **the perfect participle of a deponent verb (active meaning: locūtus = having spoken)**. *Haec locūta, Ariadna …* — having said this, Ariadne …; *fīlum secūtus* — having followed the thread. This is the only 'having done' participle Latin has, so writers use it constantly to tell what someone did just before the main verb. Latin name: *participium perfectī verbī dēpōnentis*.
English says *having spoken*, *having set out* — a participle for an action the same person finished first.
Participle stem + -us -a -um, agreeing with the person who did the action; translate 'having …-ed'.

invented.en: The boy, having slipped from the bed, cries.

core.text: *Locūtus* and *laudātus* look identical, but **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudātus = praised)** of an ordinary verb is passive. Check the dictionary form: a verb whose infinitive ends in -ī / -ārī / -ērī / -īrī is deponent, and its participle is active — *profecta* is 'having set out', not 'having been set out'.

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: A deponent verb builds its participle like any other verb but means the opposite by it: **the perfect participle of a deponent verb (active meaning: locūtus = having spoken)** describes the person who did something, not the person it was done to. *Puer lāpsus surrēxit* — the boy, having slipped, got up. He did the slipping himself; nobody slipped him.

check.ask: Which word says what Julius himself had done?

teach.title: Built exactly like the other perfect participle
teach.say: There is no new form to learn. It is the last part of the deponent's dictionary entry with the endings of *bonus*: *loquī, locūtus*; *sequī, secūtus*; *complectī, complexus*. So *Lȳdia secūta* is a woman who has followed, and *Aemilia complexa* a woman who has embraced.

check.ask: Fill in the man's form and the woman's form.

teach.title: It agrees with the doer, in the plural too
teach.say: The participle always agrees with whoever did the thing: *nautae ēgressī*, sailors who have gone out; *puellae secūtae*, girls who have followed. Count the people, look at whether they are men or women, and the ending follows by itself.

check.ask: Fill in the two plural subject forms.

teach.title: The same shape, the opposite meaning
teach.say: *laudātus* and *locūtus* end alike and look alike, and they mean opposite things. *laudātus* was praised by somebody else; *locūtus* did the speaking himself. Only the verb behind the word decides, so the deponents have to be known by name: *loquor, sequor, patior, vereor, proficīscor, lābor*.

check.ask: *veritus* — was Marcus feared, or was he afraid?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Because it means something active, it keeps everything the verb itself would take: an object (*patrem veritus*, *multa passus*), or even a whole reported clause (*dominum abesse arbitrātus*). Read it as 'having …ed', keep its object with it, and the sentence unwinds.

check.ask: *intueor, intuērī, intuitus sum*. Put in the word that says Julia herself had gazed at the mirror.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 22) set out the gap: ordinary verbs have a present active and a perfect passive participle only; deponents have present active (*loquēns*) and perfect active (*locūtus*). Their examples: *puer lāpsus* (the boy having slipped), *fēmina profecta*, *canēs secūtī*, *virōs operātōs*.
